name: Extended water fasting

card.summary: Multi-day water-only fasts for fast scale loss; much early loss is lean tissue and refeeding carries documented risks.
card.note: Refeeding syndrome and electrolyte disturbances are documented risks.

quick.overview:
An extended water fast means eating nothing and drinking only water for several days. It is discussed in forums as a shortcut to leanness.

Weight loss is quick at first, but about two-thirds of early loss is reported as lean tissue, and there are no trials on appearance outcomes.
quick.mechanism: The body first makes glucose from protein and stores, then shifts to ketosis, using ketones as fuel while minerals such as sodium and potassium fall.
quick.risks: Documented risks include electrolyte imbalance, gallstones and refeeding syndrome after about 4 to 5 days or more without food, which can be potentially fatal.

lead: Extended or prolonged water fasting means consuming no food and only water, sometimes with added electrolytes, for more than 24 hours; the clinical literature typically studies fasts of five to twenty days [1][2]. In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as a way to drop body fat and water weight quickly, reveal a leaner face and waist, and reset to a lower starting point before a cut or lean bulk, usually in attempts of two to seven days [3][4][5].

Human trials of prolonged fasting report large rises in circulating ketones, weight loss of about 2 to 10 percent, and consistent falls in blood pressure, with roughly two-thirds of the weight lost being lean mass and one-third fat mass [2]. Wikipedia documents the risks of refeeding syndrome, electrolyte imbalance and gallstones [1][8]. An international Delphi panel defined short-term fasting as two to three days and prolonged fasting as four or more consecutive days, vocabulary that forum posters use informally [6].

The practice has a long history in religion, medicine and alternative health, from supervised hospital fasts to early twentieth-century fasting-cure literature, and its best-known documented case is the 382-day medically monitored fast of Angus Barbieri in 1965 to 1966 [1][9].

chain: Fast scale weight loss and a leaner-looking face
angle.text: People use multi-day water fasts to drop body weight quickly and reveal a leaner face and waist before a cut. Trials report weight loss of 2 to 10 percent over 5 to 20 days, with both fat and lean tissue contributing.

infobox: About 2 to 10 percent over 5 to 20 days [2]
About two-thirds lean mass, one-third fat mass in trials [2]
Prolonged fasting = 4 or more consecutive days (2024 Delphi consensus) [6]

paras: A water fast allows water, and in some programs non-caloric electrolytes, with no calories. A 2024 Delphi consensus of 38 experts defined fluid-only fasting separately from modified fasting (up to 25 percent of energy needs), alternate-day fasting and fasting-mimicking diets, set short-term fasting at two to three days and prolonged fasting at four or more consecutive days, and treated intermittent fasting as repeated fasts of up to 48 hours [6]. Wikipedia describes prolonged fasting as beyond 24 hours, typically 5 to 20 days [1].
Forum posters use 'water fast' for anything from one to seven days, and often alongside calorie deficits, cuts and lean bulks [3][4][5].

Early in a fast the body draws on glycogen and then on gluconeogenesis, and later shifts into ketosis in which ketones replace glucose as the main fuel of the central nervous system [1]. Sodium, potassium and magnesium fall markedly, and hyponatremia is possible; some supervised programs use electrolyte supplements [1].

Wikipedia reports average weight loss of about 0.9 kg per day in the first week and about 0.3 kg per day by the third week, with roughly two-thirds of early loss being lean tissue and a later fat-to-lean ratio of about 7:6 [1].

A 2024 narrative review of human trials found that fasts of 5 to 20 days produce potent increases in circulating ketones and weight loss of 2 to 10 percent, with about two-thirds lean mass and one-third fat mass. The authors called the lean-mass share a concern because it suggests increased breakdown of muscle protein [2].

The same review notes that blood pressure fell consistently, fasting glucose, insulin and HbA1c fell in people with normal glycaemia, glucoregulatory markers were unchanged in people with diabetes, and effects on blood lipids were less clear [2]. A randomized trial reported that prolonged fasting outperformed short-term fasting for glucose tolerance and insulin release [7]. Trials measure weight, blood pressure and metabolic markers rather than facial appearance [2].

The 2024 Nutrition Reviews narrative review summarises human trials of prolonged water fasting for body weight, blood pressure, lipids and glycaemic control, and examines refeeding [2]. A British Journal of Nutrition randomized trial compared prolonged and short-term fasting for glucose tolerance and insulin release [7]. The Cell Metabolism terminology consensus came from an international panel of researchers and clinicians [6]. A 2015 trial of a periodic diet that mimics fasting examined a reduced-calorie alternative rather than water-only fasting [11]. Wikipedia notes that there is no sound clinical evidence that fasting extends human longevity, and describes a review reporting improved alertness and mood in some fasting studies [1]. No controlled trial has measured the effect of extended water fasting on facial appearance.

Wikipedia states that reintroducing too much food after about four to five days without eating can cause refeeding syndrome, with low potassium, magnesium and phosphate and potentially fatal complications [1][8]. The refeeding article says onset is typically within about four days of restarting food, that heart-rhythm disturbances are the most common cause of death, and that UK NICE guidance lists little or no intake for over five or ten days among its risk criteria [8].

Fasting raises gallstone risk through reduced gallbladder motility and cholesterol-saturated bile during rapid weight loss [1]. The trial-based review flags the large lean-mass share of loss [2]. Wikipedia also reports early twentieth-century deaths under fasting regimens run by Linda Hazzard, and quotes physician Morris Fishbein's 1932 statement that prolonged fasting is never necessary and invariably does harm [1].

Fasting has a long religious and medical history, and Wikipedia's article covers fasting in several traditions, in peri-operative care and in alternative medicine [1]. In 1911 Upton Sinclair published The Fasting Cure, which Wikipedia says made sweeping claims about curing diseases [1]. Hippocrates and later writers described deaths when people ate after prolonged starvation, which the refeeding literature treats as an early record of that syndrome [8].

Angus Barbieri of Tayport, Scotland, entered Maryfield Hospital in Dundee in 1965 aged 27 and fasted for 382 days, from 14 June 1965 to 30 June 1966, mostly at home with outpatient monitoring. He took vitamins, electrolytes, yeast and zero-calorie drinks, and fell from about 207 kg to 82 kg [9]. Doctors reintroduced food gradually, with salt and then sugar over ten days before solid food. The case was written up in the Postgraduate Medical Journal in 1973 by Stewart and Fleming, and a 1973 study found he maintained about 89 kg [9]. The 1971 Guinness Book of Records listed it as the longest fast; Guinness does not encourage fasting records [9].

Posters ask whether to start a cut with a two to three day water fast; some replies predict a binge after breaking the fast and suggest a modest daily deficit instead, while the original poster says he would not binge [4]. Another thread, started as a joke, features a poster planning a seven-day fast while weight training and replies saying he would not last, with a reply joking about an 'oxygen fast' for a lean face [5]. Threads also ask about water fasting while on semaglutide [3]. On T Nation, a member's cutting log describes low energy but steady scale progress [10].
Related discussion covers intermittent fasting and time-restricted eating, which clinical trials have studied in groups at risk of type 2 diabetes [12].

Related practices include intermittent fasting, time-restricted eating, alternate-day fasting, modified fasting and fasting-mimicking diets [6][11][12]. GLP-1 drugs such as semaglutide slow gastric emptying, which clinical reviews discuss in the context of procedures and fasting [13].

timeline.event: Upton Sinclair publishes The Fasting Cure [1].
Physician Morris Fishbein states that prolonged fasting is never necessary and invariably does harm [1].
Angus Barbieri begins a medically monitored fast that runs 382 days, to June 1966 [1][9].
The Guinness Book of Records lists Barbieri's fast as the longest [9].
Stewart and Fleming's case report and a follow-up study describe his weight maintenance [9].
Trial of a fasting-mimicking diet reported in Cell Metabolism [11].
Randomized trial compares prolonged and short-term fasting for glucose tolerance [7].
International Delphi consensus defines fasting terms, and a narrative review summarises prolonged water-fasting trials [2][6].

lore.intro: Water fasting appears in forums as a fast route to a leaner face, often debated against a steady deficit [4][5].

claims.claim: A multi-day water fast removes fat faster than a calorie deficit.
claims.believers: Posters planning two to seven day fasts say they want quick results before cutting [4][5].
claims.experts: Trials report 2 to 10 percent weight loss with about two-thirds from lean mass; risks include refeeding syndrome and electrolyte imbalance [1][2].

claims.claim: A short fast gives a leaner face quickly.
claims.believers: A thread title and replies frame water fasting as the way to a lean face and physique [5].
claims.experts: Trials measure weight, blood pressure and glycaemic markers rather than facial appearance, and early loss includes glycogen and water [1][2].

claims.claim: Fasting a few days before a cut is a clean way to start.
claims.believers: Original posters ask about two to three days to start a cut and say they will not binge afterward [4].
claims.experts: Other posters predict a binge and suggest a 300 kcal daily deficit; the review notes refeeding effects were examined in few trials [4][2].

claims.claim: Water fasting can be combined with semaglutide.
claims.believers: Users ask whether anyone has tried it [3].
claims.experts: GLP-1 drugs slow gastric emptying, and clinical reviews discuss the consequences; no trial of combined use has been published [13].

claims.claim: Fasting is mainly a detox or longevity practice.
claims.believers: Early twentieth-century fasting-cure literature such as Upton Sinclair's The Fasting Cure promoted fasting for cleansing and disease cure [1].
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports no sound clinical evidence that fasting extends human longevity, and describes detoxification claims as lacking scientific basis [1].
